title: Design a distributed rate limiter.
description: Rate limiting system with per-user and per-API limits across multiple servers using Redis.

data.text: **Question:** Design a distributed rate limiter that works across multiple servers.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Per-user rate limits (e.g., 100 requests per minute)
Support for different time windows (second, minute, hour)
Graceful degradation when the rate limiter is unavailable
Burst allowance for legitimate traffic spikes

data.text: Three common algorithms are token bucket, leaky bucket, and fixed window counter. Each has different trade-offs for burst handling, memory usage, and distributed accuracy.

data.caption: Distributed rate limiter architecture with Redis

data.title: Clock Skew
data.text: Distributed rate limiters are sensitive to clock skew between servers. Use Redis sorted sets with timestamps rather than relying on local clocks.

data.title: Common Edge Cases
items: Distributed Redis node failures and failover
Clock skew between rate limiter instances
Backend service unavailable while Redis is healthy
High cardinality keys causing Redis memory pressure

cards.title: Token Bucket
cards.description: Tokens accumulate at a fixed rate. Requests consume tokens. Allows bursts up to bucket capacity.

cards.title: Leaky Bucket
cards.description: Requests queue and are processed at a fixed rate. Smooths traffic but adds latency.

cards.title: Fixed Window
cards.description: Counts requests in fixed time windows. Simple but vulnerable to boundary bursts.

data.title: Horizontal Scaling Strategies
items: Use Redis cluster with consistent hashing for key distribution
Set TTL on all counters to prevent unbounded memory growth
Replicate Redis for read-heavy workloads and high availability
Cache rate limit rules locally with periodic refresh
Implement fallback to local counters when Redis is unavailable

items.question: How do you prevent Redis from becoming a bottleneck?
items.answer: Use Redis cluster sharding, pipeline multiple commands, and implement local caching with eventual consistency for non-critical limits.

items.question: How do you handle rate limiting for authenticated versus anonymous users?
items.answer: Use user ID for authenticated users and IP address for anonymous users. Apply stricter limits to anonymous traffic to prevent abuse.

items.question: What happens when Redis goes down?
items.answer: Implement a fail-open or fail-closed strategy based on risk tolerance. For critical APIs, fail-closed with cached rules. For less critical APIs, fail-open with local counters.

items.question: How do you handle microservice-to-microservice rate limiting?
items.answer: Use mTLS-based service identity and apply rate limits per service account. Consider circuit breakers in addition to rate limiting.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Token bucket is the most common algorithm for flexible rate limiting
Redis provides atomic operations needed for distributed counters
Always set TTLs on counters to prevent memory leaks
Implement graceful degradation when the rate limiter is unavailable
Use different strategies for user-based and IP-based limits
data.takeaway: Distributed rate limiters require atomic operations, careful clock handling, and graceful degradation to remain accurate under high concurrency.
